I've been working out every 3 days for a few weeks now and I've been eating more, but I feel fatter. I haven't been eating sugary things and have been eating mostly healthy foods (the worst foods being mac and cheese and Honey Bunches of Oats). I've been trying to get a good mix of protein, fats, and carbohydrates. Do you normally feel fatter even if you are gaining muscle weight or should I try to decrease my carbohydrate intake even more?

If your gaining fat but not muscle, increase protein consumption, decrease other forms of caloric consumption (fats and carbs)

When I bulk I don't really ever feel fatter but then I try to keep my diet mostly clean when I bulk. But if you feel you are getting fatter and do not want that result then yes decrease your carbohydrate intake a little AND increase your protein intake

I'm not looking fatter, I just feel a bit fatter. I'll try replacing some of the carbohydrates with protein. Would another solution be to get more carbohydrates from fruits and vegetables and less from grains, or does it not make much of a difference (I eat both, but I get more from grains)?
It doesn't make much of a difference. Because in the end it's the total number of calories in that matter.

What exactly does "feel" fatter mean? Maybe you are just feeling more full throughout the day because you are eating more than you are used to. As to fruits/veges vs. grains that's something you got to experiment with. I personally don't prefer starchy or grainy carbs and like to make smoothies with just fruit and vegetables for my carbs. Everything is really based on your individual body and what you like and work best with.

By "a good mix," exactly what are you shooting for as far as daily protein intake? Chances are it's still not enough. A good go-to rule is generally "eat more," especially in regard to lean protein. Go to Aldi, get a family sized bag each of chicken breast and salmon. Maybe add cottage cheese as a snack throughout the day, too; adding fruit, like pineapple, is optional. That one's kind-of hit or miss as far as personal preference, but I grew up eating it. I looked at a nutrition label recently and was pleasantly shocked at the protein content. As far as decreasing your carb intake, just depends on what you're comfortable with. For myself, I feel like carbs translate directly to energy, so I try to set a healthy medium. I feel absolutely drained when I cut carbs, but I might just be a wuss, haha.

Feeling fat is usually a matter of water weight. Watch your sodium intake. The fix for this is to actually drink more water. Generally, make sure you're not going more than about 500 Kcals over your TDEE. I usually suggest only eating the extra calories on the days you workout. If you're just beginning, the extra calories are probably not needed. The first 2 or 3 months you are mostly training your nervous system and the calories are not necessary.

I'm not a delivery person, but when I was in the military, they pushed volunteering a LOT... and one of the things I volunteered for a couple of times was Meals On Wheels.

We would drive door-to-door and bring free lunches to less-fortunate or less-capable people around town. It was nice, and helped us give back to the community.

Well, one day, I brought a lunch to a TINY, ratty apartment and knocked on the door. The man that answered was totally bare-assed naked, and it looked like he had dried blood and vomit all over his MASSIVE stomach. Working in the medical field, but not being a medical doctor, it looked to me as if his leg wasn't getting the diabetic circulation it needed, and it was on its way out.

But that wasn't even the first thing that struck me... the smell hit me like a truck before I even saw him. It was a mix of bigfoot's shit and burning, rotten shrimp. When he opened up the door, it poured out like it was trying to escape that apartment due because even IT was disgusted by what was behind the door.

He seemed like a nice guy, and he smiled and thanked me for the lunch, and I smiled back and told him he was welcome, but it was all I could do to not throw up all over his feet.

Thank you for replying, but I would like to point out that as serving in the military you really shouldn't feel a need to give back to the community, you're already giving by your service. I mean you should volunteer if your want to, but damn I think you already give.

Thank you. It wasn't such a bad thing, and it helped put the fact that we were there to serve the community into perspective. The civilians pay us through their tax dollars, so we give back to the civilians. It was the kind of situation where we kind of had to do it, but we got to choose what we wanted to volunteer for, and when we wanted to do it.

If I didn't want to volunteer, I could just do nothing... but I'd never have been promoted, and I probably would have been discharged... although I don't know of that ever happening. So, it was mandatory, but not, if that makes sense.

But you could volunteer to work with with children at a local elementary school, help build houses for Habitat for Humanity, or liason for the Make a Wish Foundation... all which I did, and chose to do. It was fun, and I'd never trade anything for it. The choices were literally endless, so it was hard to find yourself in a position where you couldn't volunteer for something that interested you.

I still find it strange that you're risking your life for our country and then when you get back to your country you're forced to volunteer, that kind of blows my mind. Any way, thank you again for your service. On a completely different note, when I see a service member at the airport or somewhere in public I always want to thank them for their service to our country. My SO says I shouldn't bc the service member finds it insulting bc I have no idea of the difficulty and terribleness they have gone through. What are your thoughts on that? How would you react to a stranger thanking you for your service to our country?

Honestly, it's always kind of awkward for me when I'm thanked. I just don't really know how to react. I just don't think I deserve to be thanked.

What I did was my job, and nothing more than that... I never thought of it as anything more than that. It was definitely a different kind of job, and I'll never be put in that situation again but, at the end of the day, it was still just a job. I griped and complained about it most day, probably like you complain about your job.

So, when people thank me, I put on a smile and always say, "No, thank you!" I just don't feel like I deserve any thanks for doing what you technically pay me for.

IMHO, I would never find it insulting or get offended if someone thanked me for my service... But I can't begin to speak for everyone in the military. Honestly, I don't think I could expect anyone to understand, but that's no reason to get offended by a well-intentioned gesture.

Some deployments are personal, and I won't ever discuss them, even with family or friends... But most deployments are just rough, with long 12-hour days, and hot dry days, and cold dry nights... And some are actually rather enjoyable.

The only reason I'd be anything more than grateful about discussing my service would be if you asked about a deployment, I told you I didn't want to discuss it, and you kept pestering me to talk about it.

So, I can't say I get offended... There's nothing to be offended about. It's more that I don't feel like I deserved to be thanked.

This probably sounds kind of stupid and doesn't rise to the level of some of these stories. Anyway, I delivered pizzas during my senior year in high school for a small local pizza place. On my very first delivery I go up to the door happy as could be about starting my new job and getting some cash. I knock, they answer, I give them their food, and I tell them it's like 24 dollars and some change. Then they give me 2 20's. At this point I realize I never thought about change. I had no cash on me. I was silent just looking at the 2 20's for what seemed like a really really long time.

Finally, I just told the lady I forgot to bring change with me. She gets a pretty angry look on her face. I offer to give the other 20 back and just take the hit of 4 or 5 dollars out of my own pocket. She says "no, just keep the extra 20," but it was in a way that I could tell she was really upset and didn't really want to give me the 20. I said something like, "No, it's ok. I'll just take the 5 dollar hit." She insisted I take the 20 so I took the 20, but I told her I'd come back with her change after I delivered all my other orders. I'm pretty sure she didn't believe that i'd come back.

After my orders were delivered I went back to the store, told the owner, and then he got me some change from the register. I did come back, I gave her the change, but I don't think we ever got anymore orders from that house again. She did tip me 5 bucks though. So thank you to her for being patient and kind.
